entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11095"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.10.1-Ezek.10.22">Eze 10:1-22</reference>. Vision of Coals of Fire Scattered over the City:</title> <div sID="gen19994" type="x-p"/> Repetition of the Vision of the Cherubim.<div eID="gen19994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19995" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11095"/>1. The throne of Jehovah appearing in the midst of the judgments implies that whatever intermediate agencies be employed, He controls them, and that the whole flows as a necessary consequence from His essential holiness (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.22">Eze 1:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26">26</reference>).<div eID="gen19995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19996" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cherubim--</hi>in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.5">Eze 1:5</reference>, called "living creatures." The repetition of the vision implies that the judgments are approaching nearer and nearer. These two visions of Deity were granted in the beginning of Ezekiel's career, to qualify him for witnessing to God's glory amidst his God-forgetting people and to stamp truth on his announcements; also to signify the removal of God's manifestation from the visible temple (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.18">Eze 10:18</reference>) for a long period (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.2">Eze 43:2</reference>). The feature (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.12">Eze 10:12</reference>) mentioned as to the cherubim that they were "full of eyes," though omitted in the former vision, is not a difference, but a more specific detail observed by Ezekiel now on closer inspection. Also, here, there is no rainbow (the symbol of mercy after the flood of wrath) as in the former; for here judgment is the prominent thought, though the marking of the remnant in <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.4">Eze 9:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6">6</reference> shows that there was mercy in the background. The cherubim, perhaps, represent redeemed humanity combining in and with itself the highest forms of subordinate creaturely life (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.20">Ro 8:20</reference>). Therefore they are associated with the twenty-four elders and are distinguished from the angels (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.1-Rev.5.14">Re 5:1-14</reference>). They stand on the mercy seat of the ark, and on that ground become the habitation of God from which His glory is to shine upon the world. The different forms symbolize the different phases of the Church. So the quadriform Gospel, in which the incarnate Saviour has lodged the revelation of Himself in a fourfold aspect, and from which His glory shines on the Christian world, answers to the emblematic throne from which He shone on the Jewish Church. <div eID="gen19996" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11096"/><div sID="gen19997" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11096"/><hi type="bold">2. he--</hi>Jehovah; He who sat on the "throne."<div eID="gen19997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the man--</hi>the Messenger of mercy becoming the Messenger of judgment (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.2">Eze 9:2</reference>). Human agents of destruction shall fulfil the will of "the Man," who is Lord of men.<div eID="gen19998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wheels--</hi>Hebrew, galgal, implying quick revolution; so the impetuous onset of the foe (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.24">Eze 23:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.10">26:10</reference>); whereas "ophan," in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.15">Eze 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference> implies mere revolution.<div eID="gen19999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">coals of fire--</hi>the wrath of God about to burn the city, as His sword had previously slain its guilty inhabitants. This "fire," how different from the fire on the altar never going out (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.12">Le 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.13">13</reference>), whereby, in type, peace was made with God! Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.33.12">Is 33:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">14</reference>. It is therefore not taken from the altar of reconciliation, but from between the wheels of the cherubim, representing the providence of God, whereby, and not by chance, judgment is to fall. <div eID="gen20000" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11097"/><div sID="gen20001" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11097"/><hi type="bold">3. right ... of ... house--</hi>The scene of the locality whence judgment emanates is the temple, to mark God's vindication of His holiness injured there. The cherubim here are not those in the holy of holies, for the latter had not "wheels." They stood on "the right of the house," that is, the south, for the Chaldean power, guided by them, had already advanced from the north (the direction of Babylon), and had destroyed the men in the temple, and was now proceeding to destroy the city, which lay south and west.<div eID="gen20001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the cherubim ... the man--</hi>There was perfect concert of action between the cherubic representative of the angels and "the Man," to minister to whom they "stood" there (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.7">Eze 10:7</reference>).<div eID="gen20002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cloud--</hi>emblem of God's displeasure; as the "glory" or "brightness" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.4">Eze 10:4</reference>) typifies His majesty and clearness in judgment. <div eID="gen20003" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11103"/><div sID="gen20013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11103"/><hi type="bold">9. wheels--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.15">Eze 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>). The things which, from <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.8">Eze 10:8</reference> to the end of the chapter, are repeated from the first chapter are expressed more decidedly, now that he gets a nearer view: the words "as it were," and "as if," so often occurring in the first chapter, are therefore mostly omitted. The "wheels" express the manifold changes and revolutions in the world; also that in the chariot of His providence God transports the Church from one place to another and everywhere can preserve it; a truth calculated to alarm the people in Jerusalem and to console the exiles [Polanus]. <div eID="gen20013" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11107"/><div sID="gen20026" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11107"/><hi type="bold">13. O wheel--</hi>rather, "they were called, whirling," that is, they were most rapid in their revolutions [Maurer]; or, better, "It was cried unto them, The whirling" [Fairbairn]. Galgal here used for "wheel," is different from ophan, the simple word for "wheel." Galgal is the whole wheelwork machinery with its whirlwind-like rotation. Their being so addressed is in order to call them immediately to put themselves in rapid motion. <div eID="gen20026" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11108"/><div sID="gen20027" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11108"/><hi type="bold">14. cherub--</hi>but in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.10">Eze 1:10</reference> it is an ox. The chief of the four cherubic forms was not the ox, but man. Therefore "cherub" cannot be synonymous with "ox." Probably Ezekiel, standing in front of one of the cherubim (namely, that which handed the coals to the man in linen), saw of him, not merely the ox-form, but the whole fourfold form, and therefore calls him simply "cherub"; whereas of the other three, having only a side view, he specifies the form of each which met his eye [Fairbairn]. As to the likelihood of the lower animals sharing in "the restoration of all things," see <reference osisRef="Isa.11.6">Is 11:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.25">65:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.20">Ro 8:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.21">21</reference>; this accords with the animal forms combined with the human to typify redeemed man. <div eID="gen20027" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11112"/><div sID="gen20034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11112"/>18. The departure of the symbol of God's presence from the temple preparatory to the destruction of the city. Foretold in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.17">De 31:17</reference>. Woe be to those from whom God departs (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.12">Ho 9:12</reference>)! Compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15">1Sa 28:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.21">4:21</reference>: "I-chabod, Thy glory is departed." Successive steps are marked in His departure; so slowly and reluctantly does the merciful God leave His house. First He leaves the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.3">Eze 9:3</reference>); He elevates His throne above the threshold of the house (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.1">Eze 10:1</reference>); leaving the cherubim He sits on the throne (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.4">Eze 10:4</reference>); He and the cherubim, after standing for a time at the door of the east gate (where was the exit to the lower court of the people), leave the house altogether (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.18">Eze 10:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.19">19</reference>), not to return till <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.2">Eze 43:2</reference>. <div eID="gen20034" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 18. The departure of the symbol of God's presence from the temple preparatory to the destruction of the city. Foretold in De 31:17 . Woe be to those from whom God departs ( Ho 9:12 )! Compare 1Sa 28:15 , 16 ; 4:21 : "I-chabod, Thy glory is departed." Successive steps are marked in His departure; so slowly and reluctantly does the merciful God leave His house. First He leaves the sanctuary ( Eze 9:3 ); He elevates His throne above the threshold of the house ( Eze 10:1 ); leaving the cherubim He sits on the throne ( Eze 10:4 ); He and the cherubim, after standing for a time at the door of the east gate (where was the exit to the lower court of the people), leave the house altogether ( Eze 10:18 , 19 ), not to return till Eze 43:2 .

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11114"/><div sID="gen20036" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11114"/>21. The repetition is in order that the people about to live without the temple might have, instead, the knowledge of the temple mysteries, thus preparing them for a future restoration of the covenant. So perverse were they that they would say, "Ezekiel fancies he saw what has no existence." He, therefore, repeats it over and over again. <div eID="gen20036" type="x-p"/>
